bib.title: MindSearch: Mimicking Human Minds Elicits Deep AI Searcher

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "MindSearch: Mimicking Human Minds Elicits Deep AI Searcher", Zehui Chen*, Kuikun Liu*, Qiuchen Wang, Jiangning Liu, Wenwei Zhang, Kai Chen, Feng Zhao (USTC, Shanghai AI Lab). Header on p1: "Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2025"; arXiv:2407.20183v2, 31 Oct 2025. Verified as the expected paper.
COVERAGE: 23 of 23 pages, 70,917 of 70,917 chars read, including appendices A-G (refs skimmed). Figures 1-10 are images, so figure contents were not seen, only captions. The system-prompt appendix (G) was read for WebPlanner and WebSearcher up to the numbered "Considerations" list.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- claim: Planning as incremental DAG construction through code (WebPlanner) beats ReAct and CodeAct as the planning strategy, with WebSearcher held fixed.
  number: ReAct 58.0, CodeAct 61.3, MindSearch 64.0, no search 37.6
  setup: HotpotQA, InternLM2.5-7b-chat, WebSearcher identical across rows, Bing only.
  quote: "Strategy Performance - 37.6 ReAct 58.0 CodeAct 61.3 Ours 64.0"
  where: Table 2, p8
- claim: Main closed-set results. MindSearch beats ReAct Search on average, and the gain is larger for the 7B open model.
  number: GPT-4o avg 59.8 vs ReAct 55.1 vs no-search 53.5. InternLM2.5-7b avg 49.2 vs ReAct 42.9 vs no-search 28.9. Stated gain: 4.7% (GPT-4o) and 6.3% (InternLM2-7b).
  setup: Bamboogle, Musique 2/3/4-hop, HotpotQA easy/medium/hard; zero-shot; HotpotQA graded by a GPT-4o judge. Bing is the only search source.
  quote: "MindSearch significantly outperforms its vanilla baselines by a large margin (4.7% on GPT-4o and 6.3% on InternLM2-7b)"
  where: Table 1 and Sec 3.2.2, p7
  note: On GPT-4o, MindSearch is not uniformly best. HotpotQA easy is 80.0 vs ReAct 81.0, and Musique 4-hop is 14.6 vs no-search 20.0 on the 2-hop column (the extraction scrambles the column order, so do not quote single cells without checking the table image). Per the text, most gains come from the hard HotpotQA set.
- claim: Each WebSearcher component contributes. Page selection removal hurts most in absolute terms, and the paper says multi-query generation has the most influence.
  number: full 64.0; w/o MQG 60.6; w/o PPC (prefix previous context) 63.3; w/o PS 58.0
  setup: InternLM2.5-7b-chat, HotpotQA.
  quote: "Ours 64.0 w/o MQG 60.6 w/o PPC 63.3 w/o PS 58.0"
  where: Table 3, p8
  note: The text says MQG has the most influence, but the table shows w/o PS is the larger drop (58.0). Flag this inconsistency in the paper.
- claim: Context is passed along graph edges. Each WebSearcher gets its parent node's response and the root question as a prefix, so the planner never sees raw pages. Removing this prefix costs little (0.7 points).
  number: 64.0 to 63.3 without PPC
  setup: as above.
  quote: "we simply prefix the response from its father node as well as the root node when executing each search agent."
  where: Sec 2.3, p5
- claim: Mechanism. Nodes added in one code step depend only on earlier nodes, so they run in parallel. Adding a node triggers a WebSearcher. The final answer is produced by adding a response node.
  number: none
  quote: "Since the newly added nodes are only dependent on nodes generated in previous steps, we can parallel them to achieve a much faster information aggregation speed."
  where: Sec 2.1, p3
- claim: Prompting the LLM to plan the whole workflow in one go does not work well, which motivates the graph and code interface.
  number: none
  quote: "merely prompting the LLM to plan the entire data workflow architecture does not yield satisfactory performance."
  where: Sec 2.1, p3
- claim: Scaling. MindSearch scales better than ReAct, with better accuracy for fewer inference steps. Single-turn search is cheapest and passes the easy level.
  number: turns capped at 10 ("limited performance gains by enlarging this hyperparameter"); the numbers are in Fig 6 only (an image). MindSearch also averages fewer queries than ReAct, 3.2 vs 3.5.
  setup: HotpotQA, InternLM2.5-7b; cost normalised to single-turn.
  quote: "MindSearch generates 0.3 fewer queries on average compared to ReAct (3.2 vs 3.5)"
  where: Sec 3.4 p8-9 and App C.2 p16
- claim: DAG depth grows with hop count, but not 1:1. Parallel execution and shortcuts keep depth low, so the DAG is shallow and wide.
  number: depth 1.1 / 1.2 / 1.6 for 2 / 3 / 4 hops
  setup: Musique, GPT-4o.
  quote: "Num Hops Depth 2 1.1 3 1.2 4 1.6"
  where: Table 5, p15
- claim: Compared with other methods, MindSearch gets the best average, including Searchain, which also builds a reasoning chain.
  number: ReAct 58.0, self-ask 58.3, CodeAct 61.3, Searchain 61.6, MindSearch 64.0 (hard: 49/49/51/54/57)
  setup: HotpotQA, InternLM2.5-7b.
  quote: "Searchain (Xu et al., 2024) 70.0 61.0 54.0 61.6 MindSearch (Ours) 69.0 66.0 57.0 64.0"
  where: Table 4, p15
- claim: Error recovery comes from the code interface. Python exceptions are fed back to the planner for regeneration. A "not found" reply from a searcher triggers a rewritten query. After several failures the planner is allowed to emit the response node, which avoids endless loops.
  number: none
  quote: "when WebPlanner generates wrong code or invalid planning sentence, we can simply validate it in the Python code interpreter and seed the exception back to the LLM for re-generation."
  where: App E.1, p16
- claim: Works with other open models, with varying quality.
  number: DeepSeek-V2 69.6, GLM4-9b 60.0, Qwen-2.5-7b 57.6
  setup: HotpotQA average, MindSearch framework.
  quote: "DeepSeek-V2 (Liu et al., 2024) 70.0 71.0 68.0 69.6"
  where: Table 6, p16
- claim: Human preference (100 real queries, 5 experts, majority vote) favours MindSearch (InternLM2.5-7b) over Perplexity Pro and ChatGPT-Web on depth and breadth. Facticity is the weaker dimension.
  number: facticity 70% vs breadth 83%
  setup: 100 curated queries; blind, shuffled; the Fig 4 bars are not in the text.
  quote: "MindSearch does not yield much better performance in terms of facticity, compared to breadth (70% vs 83%)."
  where: Sec 3.1.2, p6
- claim: Speed claims. These are headline figures, and the paper does not show how they were measured.
  number: >300 pages in under 3 min vs about 3 h for a human; 10 questions: 19h17min (5 humans) vs 23 min.
  quote: "Human labelers spend 19h17min to accomplish the search tasks while MindSearch only takes 23 min."
  where: App B, p15 and abstract
- claim: Separating planner and searcher keeps both contexts small.
  number: none (claimed, not ablated)
  quote: "WebPlanner can purely focus on the decomposition and analysis of the user question without being distracted by the over-length web search results."
  where: Sec 2.3, p5

LIMITS
- The authors concede that citation quality is not evaluated. The system takes no visual input and cannot interact with web pages (browse or click). The facticity gain is small, and they suspect long context distraction.
- They never show that the graph structure itself drives the gain, beyond Table 2. Table 2 changes the action space (code to graph) and the interface at the same time.
- The benchmarks are mostly 2-4 hop QA with a GPT-4o judge on HotpotQA. The open-set test has only 100 queries and 5 raters, with no variance reported. The ablations use one 7B model.
- Fig 6 holds the cost numbers (not in the text). The time claims (3 min, 23 min) give no hardware, parallelism or API-latency details.
- The planner only adds nodes and edges, with no pruning or merging. The paper does not discuss cycles, since the graph is a DAG by construction.
- The 2024 baselines (GPT-4o, o1-era) have dated.

BUILDS ON: ReAct (Yao et al., 2022b); CodeAct (Wang et al., 2024); self-ask (Press et al., 2022); Search-in-the-Chain (Xu et al., 2024, Searchain); RQ-RAG (Chan et al., 2024); Self-RAG (Asai et al., 2023); WebGPT (Nakano et al., 2021); WebGLM (Liu et al., 2023); RAG (Lewis et al., 2020); test-time scaling (Snell et al., 2024); benchmarks Bamboogle (Press et al., 2022), Musique (Trivedi et al., 2022), HotpotQA (Yang et al., 2018).

CODE (verbatim from the App G WebPlanner system prompt, pp22-23)
- "Class: WebSearchGraph ... This class manages nodes and edges of a web search graph and conducts searches via a web proxy."
- Methods listed (underscores are lost in the extraction): add_root_node(node_content, node_name='root'); add_node(node_name, node_content) returns the search results; add_response_node(node_name='response'); add_edge(start_node, end_node); reset(); node(node_name).
- Rules: "4. When adding a response node, add it separately; do not add a response node and other nodes simultaneously." "5. In a single output, do not include multiple code blocks; only one code block per output."
- Format: "<|action start|><|interpreter|> ```python ...```<|action end|>"
- WebSearcher rule: "The citation format is [[int]]."

FIGURES
- Fig 1 (p2): framework overview, WebPlanner orchestrating several WebSearchers. Good for a topology diagram.
- Fig 2 (p4): a worked trace of planning as coding, with thoughts and code per turn. Shows dynamic graph growth best.
- Fig 3 (p5): WebSearcher pipeline, at most 4 steps: query rewrite, search aggregation, page selection, summarization.
- Fig 6 (p8): inference cost vs performance for single-turn, ReAct and MindSearch. Holds the scaling numbers.
- Figs 7-9 (p17-18): error recovery examples. Fig 4 and 5 (p6): human-eval bars and a trajectory comparison.

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions found. The extraction scrambles the Table 1 column order and drops underscores in the code names. Figures 1-10 were not viewed as images. The paper is a single planner with parallel leaf searchers, so it is a planner/worker pattern with a dynamically grown DAG rather than a general graph topology study.
